cards.title: Deciding whether an exact MMS allocation exists
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Determine the computational complexity of deciding whether an explicitly given finite instance of indivisible goods with nonnegative additive valuations has a complete maximin-share allocation. The number of agents varies with the input. The exact decision predicate is defined below; the classification or bound precision requested by the imported question remains to be specified.
cards.why: Distinguishes the complexity of attaining a fairness guarantee from the difficulty of evaluating each agent's benchmark.

cards.definitions: An input consists of a list of n≥1 agents, a list G of m≥0 goods, and an explicit n-by-m table of nonnegative integers vᵢg written in binary. Input length N counts these lists and all value bits. Agent i assigns a bundle S⊆G the additive value vᵢ(S)=∑g∈S vᵢg, with vᵢ(∅)=0. Let Πₙ(G) be the finite set of labeled partitions (P₁,…,Pₙ) of all goods into n disjoint bundles; empty bundles are allowed. Define μᵢ=maxP∈Πₙ(G) min1≤j≤n vᵢ(Pⱼ). Each agent uses her own valuation for every bundle in this benchmark partition. A complete allocation is A∈Πₙ(G), and the input is a yes-instance exactly when some A satisfies vᵢ(Aᵢ)≥μᵢ for every i. A zero benchmark imposes the inequality vᵢ(Aᵢ)≥0 and involves no division. Benchmark values are not supplied as part of the input. There are no connectivity constraints, arrivals, transfers, discarded goods or fractional allocations. Computation uses the usual deterministic bit-cost model unless a complexity class explicitly permits nondeterminism or an oracle. The nonnegative rational binary-value version has the same polynomial-time classification: each agent’s row can be scaled by a positive common denominator of polynomial bit length without changing the fairness inequalities.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a proved classification or matching bounds for this exact existence decision predicate, under an explicitly fixed precision and reduction convention. The source import does not yet fix that requested precision, so the card remains an incomplete computational benchmark. Hardness of computing μᵢ, finding an optimal allocation, or solving a constrained variant does not by itself classify this yes/no predicate.

context_blocks.title: Choose a partition, receive its least valuable bundle
context_blocks.text: An agent’s maximin share is what she can guarantee by dividing the goods into n bundles and then taking the bundle she values least. Each agent may prefer a different partition. The question is whether a single allocation can simultaneously meet all these personal guarantees.

context_blocks.title: An example and an important distinction
context_blocks.text: For two agents who both value three goods at 4, 3 and 3, each maximin share is 4. Giving one agent the first good and the other the last two meets both benchmarks, although the first agent receives less than her proportional share of 5. Identical valuations always admit an MMS allocation by the definition of an optimal common partition. Consequently, difficulty in computing that partition need not make its existence difficult to decide.

context_blocks.title: What is known about the decision problem
context_blocks.text: The 2023 survey states that NP-hardness is unknown for general nonnegative additive goods valuations. The existence problem has a Δ₂ᴾ upper bound, also recorded in the 2020 work on the broader graph-constrained model. Here Δ₂ᴾ=Pᴺᴾ means deterministic polynomial time with an oracle answering NP decision questions. This upper bound does not give an ordinary polynomial-time algorithm.

context_blocks.title: Nearby hardness results concern different tasks
context_blocks.text: Maximin share and minimax share reverse the order of the minimum and maximum and need not agree. Likewise, computing a fair allocation under an existence promise is a search problem. The August 2026 temporal preprint studies fairness after every round of irreversible arrivals. Hardness in any of these settings cannot be transferred to the static unconstrained existence question without an appropriate reduction.

context_blocks.title: Why a classification matters
context_blocks.text: An exact allocation need not exist when agents value goods differently. Understanding how hard it is to detect existence would separate the cost of evaluating a fairness benchmark from the cost of deciding whether the benchmarks can coexist. It would also clarify when a failure to find an exact allocation reflects computational difficulty rather than an impossible demand.

cards.definitions: An instance consists of a finite set G of m≥0 indivisible goods and n agents. Each number vᵢg is a nonnegative real, and vᵢ(S)=∑g∈S vᵢg for S⊆G. Let Πd(G) denote all labeled partitions (P₁,…,Pd) of G into d pairwise disjoint bundles, allowing empty bundles. The 1-out-of-d maximin share of agent i is μᵢ(d)=maxP∈Πd(G) min1≤j≤d vᵢ(Pⱼ). The maximum is attained because the set of partitions is finite. A complete allocation A belongs to Πₙ(G): every good goes to exactly one agent, with no copies, payments, disposal or fractional goods. Define Dₙ as the set of positive integers d such that for every m and every valuation table there exists such an A with all n inequalities. Then d*(n)=min Dₙ. Increasing d weakens each benchmark. Known universal upper bounds make Dₙ nonempty, so this minimum is attained. The quantifiers are ∀n, choose d*(n), then ∀instances, ∃allocation; d may not depend on the number or values of the goods. This is an existence extremum, with no computation-time or preference-query restriction.
cards.answer_criterion: Give the exact function d*(n) for all positive integers n, with a universal existence proof at the proposed value and a matching impossibility proof for every smaller positive denominator. By monotonicity, when d*(n)>1 a counterexample at d*(n)−1 suffices for the latter part. An improved upper bound, an asymptotic leading constant, or a result permitting additional copies does not determine the requested exact function.

context_blocks.title: Relax the number of benchmark bundles
context_blocks.text: An agent imagines dividing all goods and then receiving her least valuable bundle. Ordinary MMS uses n bundles, one per real agent. Using a larger imaginary number d lowers the required share, while the actual allocation still has n recipients. The question is how little this benchmark must be weakened to make it universally achievable.

context_blocks.title: A small example
context_blocks.text: If an agent values each of six goods at 1, her 1-out-of-2 share is 3 and her 1-out-of-3 share is 2. Those numbers describe her personal benchmarks, not how many agents must actually receive goods. Different agents can value the same goods differently, so their best benchmark partitions need not coincide.

context_blocks.title: What ordinal means here
context_blocks.text: The fairness comparison is determined by each agent’s ranking of complete bundles. It is preserved if that ranking stays the same. Knowing only an ordering of individual goods does not generally determine the ordering of their sums. Thus this question does not assume an algorithm receives only individual-item rankings.

context_blocks.title: The known denominator bounds
context_blocks.text: For n≥2 the checked results give d*(n)≤min{2n−2, ⌊3n/2⌋, 4⌈n/3⌉}; retaining the minimum handles rounding for small n. The last bound comes from the 2024 result. Trivially d*(1)=1 and d*(n)≥n: with only d<n goods valued at 1 by everyone, a 1-out-of-d guarantee would require a good for every agent. The exact universal denominator remains undetermined.

context_blocks.title: Why the exact threshold matters
context_blocks.text: An exact answer would identify how much competition an indivisible-resource fairness benchmark must tolerate before everyone can be protected. Recent work combines ordinal shares with envy guarantees in restricted preference classes. Those additional guarantees are useful, but they do not settle the unrestricted denominator function asked for here.

sentences: An agent’s 1-out-of-d maximin share is the best least-bundle value she can achieve by partitioning all goods into d bundles.
The allocation itself still distributes the goods among n actual agents.
The question asks for the smallest denominator that guarantees every agent her corresponding share in every additive goods instance.
Known bounds allow roughly four benchmark bundles for every three agents, with separate rounding improvements for smaller n.
Determining the exact denominator would describe the strongest universally attainable fairness standard of this form.

cards.title: Do EFkX allocations exist for a universal constant k?
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed integer k≥1 such that, for every n≥1, every finite set G of goods, and every table of nonnegative additive valuations vᵢ, there is a complete allocation (A₁,…,Aₙ) for which vᵢ(Aᵢ)≥vᵢ(Aⱼ∖S) for all agents i,j and every S⊆Aⱼ with |S|=min{k,|Aⱼ|}?

cards.definitions: For agent i, each good g has a nonnegative real value vᵢg and every bundle B⊆G has value vᵢ(B)=∑g∈B vᵢg; the empty bundle has value zero. A complete allocation partitions all goods into n labeled, disjoint bundles, possibly empty. Each good goes to exactly one agent. The displayed condition is envy-freeness up to any k goods, abbreviated EFkX: each comparison uses the potentially envious agent i’s values on both sides. The removed set S is hypothetical and is chosen universally, not chosen by the allocation algorithm to make the inequality easier. Actual goods are not removed or discarded. If |Aⱼ|≤k, the comparison is automatically satisfied because its right side is zero; this agrees with treating the source’s k-item condition as vacuous for shorter bundles. Zero-valued goods count as goods and may belong to S. The constant k is chosen before the instance and is independent of n, the number of goods and all values. This is exact existence; it imposes no efficiency requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that at least one universal constant k satisfies the stated existence claim, or prove its negation: for every integer k≥1 there is a finite additive goods instance such that every complete allocation violates at least one of its required inequalities. A counterexample for one k, or an allocation with a multiplicative factor below 1, does not resolve this quantifier structure.

context_blocks.title: How much envy can indivisibility explain?
context_blocks.text: One indivisible valuable item can prevent exact envy-freeness. EFkX allows a bounded number of items in the envied bundle to account for that discrepancy. It requires envy to disappear even after deleting the least helpful k items from the envious agent’s perspective. The question is whether some fixed allowance works for arbitrarily many agents.

context_blocks.title: Any removal versus a favorable removal
context_blocks.text: Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 5 and another bundle’s three goods at 6, 1 and 1. Removing its 6-valued good eliminates her envy, but removing either 1-valued good leaves value 7, so the pair fails EF1X. It also fails EF2X: removing the two 1-valued goods leaves value 6. This illustrates why an existential choice of removed goods is a different, weaker condition.

context_blocks.title: The connection to EFX
context_blocks.text: For k=1 this is the usual any-item EFX condition, including zero-valued items. A universal EFX existence theorem would answer this question positively. This card permits any fixed k, so it asks for a weaker universal guarantee. Choosing k separately for each instance, for example as its total number of goods, would make the property vacuous and is excluded.

context_blocks.title: Exact results for a fixed number of agents
context_blocks.text: The AAAI 2025 result establishes EF2X for four agents, in a valuation class that includes additive goods. That is a concrete exact existence theorem. It fixes the number of agents and therefore does not supply the universal constant-k guarantee for unrestricted n.

context_blocks.title: The 2026 approximation result
context_blocks.text: The May 2026 preprint gives (k+1)/(k+2)-EFkX allocations for every fixed k≥2 and any number of agents. This relaxes the inequality to vᵢ(Aᵢ)≥αvᵢ(Aⱼ∖S), where α<1. Although α approaches 1 as k grows, no finite k in that theorem attains exact fairness. Its negative graph-orientation results additionally restrict who may receive a good.

sentences: EFkX compares each agent’s bundle with another bundle after any k of that other bundle’s goods are hypothetically removed.
The same agent’s valuation is used on both sides, and all actual goods must still be allocated.
The question asks whether one constant k works for every number of agents and every nonnegative additive goods instance.
Exact guarantees are known for limited numbers of agents, while a 2026 preprint obtains multiplicative approximate guarantees for arbitrary n.
A resolution would determine whether a bounded item allowance can always account for the envy caused by indivisibility.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
